why: Horizontal flight is not the phase singled out; avoid low turns over villages during the climb.
Descent is not the phase asked about; the bank specifically identifies climb as the phase for avoiding low turns.
During climb, low turns over villages expose residents to noise and should be avoided.
Approach is not the phase asked about; climb is the keyed phase for avoiding low turns.
60-001.note: Climb straight where safe; turn only after gaining adequate height.

why: Slow changes of direction do not replace routing around villages or crossing them at sufficient altitude.
Circumnavigate settlements and cross only with adequate height, limiting noise while preserving obstacle clearance.
Low propeller RPM alone is not the prescribed route and cannot justify flying low over villages.
A low, fast passage over villages increases exposure and conflicts with noise-abatement practice.
A low approach contradicts the high-approach profile, even if power is low and configuration is late.
A high approach, low practicable power, late descent/configuration and established route minimise noise without a shortcut.
Early landing configuration and a direct approach increase low-level exposure and may leave the established route.
Normal power, early configuration and the shortest route do not follow the keyed quiet-arrival profile.
Throttle pumping does not cause inadequate power; excess priming fuel can ignite instead.
Pumping can over-prime a cold piston engine, allowing fuel in the intake to ignite as a carburettor fire.
Oil dilution is not the immediate hazard caused by pumping the throttle during starting.
Carburettor icing is not the fire hazard from pumping; excess fuel may ignite in the intake.
60-004.note: Avoid unnecessary throttle pumping during start.

why: Smoke may result from a fire but is not the specific engine-start danger identified by the bank.
A cable fire is not the typical engine-start hazard; the keyed risk is fuel ignition at the carburettor.
Sparking alone is not the named danger; combustible mixture can ignite and cause a carburettor fire.
Fuel introduced into the intake during starting can ignite, making carburettor fire the relevant hazard.
60-005.note: Use the aircraft’s prescribed starting procedure.

why: A carburettor-fire origin does not make restarting safe; the engine has already been on fire.
Taxiing still requires restarting the fire-damaged engine and risks reignition.
Do not restart an engine that was on fire; reignition could occur even after the initial fire appears out.
Altitude does not remove the danger of reignition after an engine fire.
60-006.note: A previous engine fire means no restart.

why: Turning off heat may reduce smoke entry but does not first isolate suspected electrical power.
For suspected instrument-panel electrical fire, switch the master off first, then use the aircraft checklist.
Shutting down the engine is not the first electrical-fire isolation step and may remove needed control power.
An extinguisher may be needed, but first isolate the suspected electrical source with the master switch.
Switching off the master isolates electrical supply and is the keyed first action for a cable fire.
Opening windows can feed a fire or worsen smoke exposure; isolate electrical power first.
Opening ventilation may draw smoke into the cockpit; it is not the first cable-fire action.
Closing the fuel valve addresses fuel supply, not the suspected electrical cable source.
60-008.note: For an electrical fire, disconnect its power source.

why: Pitot/window heating is not the immediate cabin-smoke control action keyed for an engine fire.
Master and ignition switches are not the specific immediate measure for smoke entering from an engine fire.
Turning heating and ventilation off limits smoke entering the cockpit, matching the keyed immediate action.
Avionics and cabin lighting do not stop smoke entering through the heating/ventilation system.
60-009.note: Use the fire-source checklist; cabin heat/air can carry smoke.

why: Master-off is the electrical-fire response, not the keyed first action for suspected engine-fire smoke.
Engine shutdown may be directed by the checklist, but this item keys turning off the heat.
Turning off heat limits smoke entering the cockpit and is the keyed action for the suspected engine fire.
Using an extinguisher is not the keyed first step; follow the engine-fire checklist.
60-010.note: Do not apply the electrical-fire response to every fire source.

why: An Alpine downslope wind is a local wind phenomenon, not the general definition of wind shear.
Wind shear is not limited to slow increases above 13,000 ft; it can occur at many altitudes.
A 15-kt threshold is not part of the definition; short-distance changes in speed or direction are shear.
Wind shear is a vertical or horizontal change in wind speed and/or direction over a short distance.
60-011.note: Shear means a rapid change in wind speed and/or direction.

why: A calm summer day alone does not provide the characteristic wind-change layer tested here.
Cold calm conditions alone are not the strongest cue; inversions can concentrate a wind change.
An inversion can create a sharp change in wind with height, making wind shear likely.
A warm front may bring weather changes, but the bank’s expected cue is an inversion.
60-012.note: Look for an inversion and rapidly changing weather.

why: An invernal warm front is not the typical associated phenomenon singled out in the bank.
Thunderstorms generate rapidly changing winds and downdrafts, so they are commonly associated with wind shear.
Fog by itself does not produce the strong wind changes characteristic of this association.
Stable high pressure generally lacks the rapid convective wind changes associated with shear.
60-013.note: Thunderstorms and heavy showers are wind-shear hazards.

why: At point 3 the aircraft exits headwind into outflow/tailwind, so airspeed falls rather than rises.
The loss of headwind or onset of tailwind at point 3 reduces indicated airspeed.
Reduced climb rate is associated especially with the downdraft core at point 2, not the keyed point-3 effect.
Point 3 does not imply a constant descent; the marked transition causes an airspeed decrease.
60-014.note: Microburst sequence: headwind gain, downdraft, then headwind loss.

why: The downdraft at point 2 opposes the aircraft’s climb and reduces its rate of climb.
The core downdraft worsens descent rather than reducing the descent rate.
A strong downdraft does not produce a constant descent rate; it degrades vertical performance.
The simplified point-2 effect is reduced climb rate with IAS approximately unchanged, not increased IAS.
60-015.note: The microburst core’s downdraft reduces climb performance.

why: An increasing headwind raises IAS and lift, tending to place the aircraft above the intended path.
The path tends higher, but increasing headwind raises rather than lowers IAS.
Both effects are reversed: the path tends higher and IAS increases.
IAS increases, but the resulting path tends higher, not lower.
60-016.note: Headwind gain: IAS rises and the approach path tends high.

why: Ground speed does not necessarily decrease; losing headwind reduces IAS and climb performance relative to the air.
A decreasing headwind does not cause TAS to increase; it removes airflow support and lowers IAS.
A headwind loss tends to put the aircraft below, not above, its expected climb path.
Decreasing headwind reduces IAS/lift, so the aircraft tends below the estimated climb path.
60-017.note: Headwind loss: expect lower IAS and a lower flight path.

why: A decreasing tailwind is equivalent to an increasing headwind, so IAS rises rather than falls.
The path tends higher, not lower, when the tailwind decreases and headwind effectively increases.
Both effects are opposite: path tends high and IAS increases.
A decreasing tailwind acts like increasing headwind, raising IAS and the approach path.
60-018.note: A tailwind decrease is a headwind increase.

why: A decreasing headwind lowers IAS and path; it does not raise either.
Headwind loss reduces IAS and lift, lowering the approach path.
The path tends lower, but IAS decreases rather than increases.
IAS decreases, but the path tends lower rather than higher.
60-019.note: Headwind loss lowers both IAS and approach path.

why: Retracting gear/flaps changes configuration during the encounter and can worsen performance; preserve configuration.
Maximum power, unchanged configuration and best-rate climb speed prioritise climb performance in the keyed response.
An improvised turn and configuration change risk losing performance and are not the keyed escape action.
Trying to accelerate away sacrifices the prescribed best-rate climb response while downdraft may overwhelm the aircraft.
60-020.note: Keyed response: max power, hold configuration, best ROC speed.

why: Avoiding take-off and landing during heavy showers or thunderstorms prevents exposure to likely severe shear.
Avoiding thermal areas is not the specific wind-shear measure and does not address storm outflow.
Choosing low altitudes near precipitation increases exposure to hazardous shear rather than avoiding it.
Mountainous terrain is not the general condition to avoid; the key hazard is storm/heavy-shower passage.
60-021.note: Avoid hazardous weather rather than attempting to penetrate it.

why: The bank keys wake onset at nosewheel lift-off, not at a fixed 15-ft altitude.
Acceleration alone does not mark onset; wake starts when the lifting aircraft becomes airborne at nosewheel lift-off.
The bank’s take-off reference is lift-off with the front gear, when the aircraft begins generating its airborne wake.
Waiting for main-gear lift-off is later than the keyed nosewheel-lift-off point.
60-022.note: Wake begins at lift-off; do not assume it starts at a particular height.

why: Low altitude does not by itself make generated vortex strongest; weight, configuration and speed are key.
A slower aircraft produces stronger wake for the same type, mass and configuration because it must generate lift at lower speed.
High altitude alone does not determine vortex strength.
Higher speed generally produces less concentrated wake than the same aircraft flying slower.
60-023.note: Heavy, clean and slow produces strong wake.

why: A slight crosswind does not reliably twist wake transversely across the runway.
The key hazard is not amplification; a light crosswind may leave a vortex on or near the runway.
A slight crosswind can drift one vortex while leaving another on or near the runway, creating a take-off hazard.
The bank does not describe faster rotation or upward drift; the concern is wake remaining near the runway.
60-024.note: A light crosswind may not clear both runway vortices.

why: This cites wake turbulence and 700 m; the keyed taxi hazard is jet blast with 200 m in this bank.
Wake is not the tested taxi hazard, and 300 m is not the keyed distance.
The keyed item concerns jet blast behind an airliner and specifies at least 200 m in the bank.
Jet blast is relevant, but 600 m is not the keyed minimum in this question.
60-025.note: Jet blast is distinct from wingtip wake; follow airport instructions.

why: Circumstances forcing the aircraft to land define an emergency landing.
“Urgent landing” is not the formal distinction tested; forced circumstances make it an emergency landing.
A precautionary landing is chosen to preserve safety before circumstances force a landing.
An outlanding describes an unprepared site, not the reason that compelled the landing.
60-026.note: Forced by circumstances = emergency; chosen early = precautionary.

why: Preserving safety by choice describes a precautionary landing, not the forced emergency definition.
Circumstances forcing the aircraft to land define an emergency landing.
Flap position does not define whether a landing is an emergency.
An emergency landing may be powered or unpowered; engine power is not the defining criterion.
60-027.note: Classify the landing by why it is happening, not flap or engine state.

why: A pilot elects to land to sustain flight safety: this is the precautionary definition.
Forced circumstances define an emergency landing, not a precautionary one.
Retracted flaps do not define a precautionary landing.
Engine-out status does not define a precautionary landing; the pilot’s safety decision does.
60-028.note: Precautionary means the pilot chooses to land before being forced.

why: When land is unreachable, flotation equipment for every occupant supports survival after ditching.
Exact waypoints may aid navigation but do not replace required survival equipment over water.
Continuous ATC contact cannot guarantee rescue and does not substitute for life jackets or a raft.
7600 indicates radio failure, not a normal over-water code or a substitute for flotation equipment.
60-029.note: If you cannot glide to land, equip every occupant to float.

why: Continuous ATC contact is useful where possible but is not the essential preparation keyed here.
Transponder-only operation is not a survival plan and does not protect occupants after ditching.
A flight plan supports search and rescue but cannot replace flotation equipment for each occupant.
Carry life vests or a life raft for all occupants when land is unlikely to be reachable.
60-030.note: Plan for survival after leaving the aircraft, not just tracking.

why: This puts configuration and declaration ahead of landing-area selection and the planned approach.
Trying to reach an airport for rescue can waste time when a suitable emergency landing site is needed.
Select a suitable area, plan the approach, complete the checklist, declare as appropriate, then focus on flying the approach.
Radio support and looking up the manual should not delay selecting a site and planning the forced approach.
60-031.note: Choose the site and plan the approach early; fly the aircraft first.

why: A specific 10 m distance is not required; inflate only after leaving the aircraft.
Inflating inside can obstruct movement through the exit and trap the occupant.
Inflate the life vest after exiting the aircraft so it cannot impede egress.
Inflating while exiting may restrict movement; wait until fully outside.
60-032.note: Inflate after egress, not inside the cabin.

why: This changes the threshold and includes frost/sand; the bank definition is >25% covered by specified contaminants >3 mm deep.
A 75% threshold is too high and omits the defined >3 mm depth condition.
More than 25% of the runway area in use covered by water, slush, snow or ice deeper than 3 mm meets the bank definition.
A 50% coverage threshold is too high; the bank’s threshold is more than 25%, with the specified depth.
60-033.note: Remember coverage, contaminants, and depth: >25%, listed material, >3 mm.

why: Wet snow increases rolling resistance; it does not primarily cause the lift decrease stated here.
Wet snow does not reduce rolling resistance; it makes the take-off roll more resistant.
Wet snow increases rolling resistance during take-off, which can degrade acceleration and performance.
Wet snow does not create an increase in lift; its tested effect is increased ground resistance.
60-034.note: Wet snow makes the take-off roll harder, not easier.

why: Wet grass increases, rather than decreases, both take-off and landing distances.
Wet grass increases ground resistance and reduces braking effectiveness, increasing both distances.
Take-off distance also increases; the option incorrectly says it decreases.
Landing distance also increases; the option incorrectly says it decreases.
60-035.note: Wet grass: longer take-off and landing distances.

why: The key danger after heavy rain is reduced braking and longer stopping, not displaced tyre markings.
Aquaplaning reduces braking effectiveness; it lengthens rather than shortens braking distance.
Glare is not the principal runway-surface danger tested after heavy rain.
Standing water can cause aquaplaning, reducing tyre contact and braking effectiveness and lengthening the stopping distance.
60-036.note: Water film can reduce tyre contact and lengthen the landing roll.

why: This describes airborne time from take-off run to touchdown, not the bank’s first-movement-to-final-rest definition.
For this bank, flight time runs from the aircraft’s first movement until it finally comes to rest at the end of the flight.
Engine start-to-shutdown includes periods outside the keyed first-movement-to-final-rest interval.
This describes a series of flights rather than the single-flight definition asked here.
60-037.note: Flight time: first movement to final rest.

why: Items 1–6 affect emitted or perceived sound; flight rules do not physically change noise, so this set is correct.
This omits RPM, gear and flap configuration, all of which can affect perceived noise.
This wrongly includes flight rules and omits RPM, gear and flap position.
This omits engine power and propeller RPM and wrongly includes flight rules.
60-038.note: Noise depends on power/RPM, configuration, track and height—not flight rules.

why: Piston-engine induction systems may have a carburettor, where excess fuel can ignite during starting.
Turbine engines do not use the piston-engine carburettor arrangement tested here.
An electric motor has no fuel carburettor to produce a carburettor fire.
A turboprop uses a turbine core; the carburettor-fire risk here concerns piston engines.
60-039.note: Carburettor fire is a piston-engine starting hazard.

why: Carbon monoxide is highly toxic and is the most dangerous listed gas in an engine-fire context.
Nitrogen is not the toxic combustion gas identified by the bank.
Oxygen supports combustion but is not the poisonous gas asked for.
Carbon dioxide can be hazardous at high concentration, but the bank keys toxic carbon monoxide.
60-040.note: CO is toxic: treat smoke as dangerous.

why: Powder is a suitable listed fire agent for several aircraft fire classes; it is not the least suitable overall.
Halon is an effective aircraft fire-extinguishing agent where approved and available.
Water is least suitable overall and can be hazardous on live electrical equipment or burning fuel.
Foam is effective for some fire classes; the bank identifies water as least suitable overall.
60-041.note: Match the extinguisher to the fire; avoid water on electrical or fuel fires.

why: Wind shear can cause sudden unexplained changes in altitude, IAS, climb rate or descent rate.
Heading or engine readings alone are not the characteristic flight-path/airspeed cues listed by the bank.
Oil pressure, temperature and engine-speed changes suggest engine trouble, not the defining wind-shear cue.
Drizzle after clear skies is not the sudden aircraft-response signature used to recognise wind shear.
60-042.note: Watch for unexplained changes in IAS, altitude, or vertical rate.

why: Retracting gear and flaps is not the keyed response; maintain configuration and adjust thrust.
Reducing speed and retracting configuration are contrary to the keyed wind-shear response.
Maintaining configuration is correct, but the response also requires adjusting thrust.
Maintain current configuration and adjust thrust; avoid large configuration changes during shear.
Microburst progression reduces, not increases, climb rate; the later outflow also lowers airspeed.
Both climb rate and airspeed do not remain increased as the aircraft moves through the microburst.
The initial IAS rise can be followed by downdraft and tailwind/outflow, reducing both climb rate and airspeed.
Climb rate decreases, but the later airspeed also decreases rather than increases.
60-044.note: A microburst can start with an IAS gain, then degrade climb and IAS.

why: Wake is not wind shear; it forms as wingtip vortices from pressure differences around a lifting wing.
Jet blast is engine exhaust and is distinct from aerodynamic wake turbulence.
Mountain-wave turbulence is terrain-related, not the wake generated by an aircraft wing.
Pressure equalisation around the wingtip creates counter-rotating vortices behind the aircraft.
60-045.note: Lift creates pressure differences that roll into wingtip vortices.

why: Propeller pitch is not the principal factor in the wake-strength rule tested here.
Temperature is not the determining factor in this bank’s wake-intensity question.
Wake intensity increases with the generating aircraft’s weight because it must generate more lift.
Altitude alone does not determine wake intensity; aircraft weight is the keyed factor.
60-046.note: Heavier aircraft generally generate stronger wake.

why: Altitude alone does not determine wake severity for otherwise identical aircraft.
At the same type, weight and configuration, the slower aircraft generates stronger wake.
Higher speed produces less concentrated wake than the slower flight condition.
Higher altitude alone does not make the aircraft’s wake more severe.
60-047.note: For the same aircraft and load, slower means stronger wake.

why: Higher altitude alone does not determine the intensity of wake turbulence.
Lower altitude alone is not the factor; speed is the relevant difference in these otherwise similar aircraft.
Higher speed is not the stronger-wake condition for the same aircraft and configuration.
The slower aircraft produces more severe wake for the same type, weight and flap setting.
60-048.note: Speed, not altitude, distinguishes the wake strength in this comparison.

why: Stay above the preceding approach path and touch down beyond its nose-gear point; a steep approach is not itself the avoidance method.
Touching down before the airliner’s point risks encountering wake; a short landing is opposite to the keyed long landing.
Touchdown is appropriately beyond the airliner’s, but a shallow approach can descend through its wake path.
A shallow approach risks crossing the wake, and stopping before its touchdown point does not avoid the vortex.
60-049.note: Land beyond the preceding aircraft’s touchdown point while staying above its path.

why: A flat direct approach does not ensure a safe site; inspect terrain and identify approach points first.
A steep approach solely for noise does not assess surface, obstacles, wind or landing options.
A rushed fast approach and quick stop neglect site investigation and can worsen landing risk.
Investigate the terrain and establish approach points and landing area before committing.
60-050.note: Survey the site and plan the approach before committing.

why: A harvested cornfield offers a short, cleared surface compared with the listed alternatives.
Long dry grass can conceal hazards and increase drag or landing distance.
Ploughed ground is rough and uneven, increasing the risk of damage or nose-over.
A village sports area may contain people and obstacles, making it unsuitable.
60-051.note: Prefer a clear, short-crop or harvested field.

why: An undisturbed lake is still a water landing and is not the most suitable land site in these choices.
Short crops offer a visible, relatively even surface; this is the most suitable listed site.
A meadow may hide uneven ground, livestock, or other hazards, unlike the visible short-crop field.
Ripe waving crops can conceal obstacles and make surface conditions difficult to judge.
60-052.note: Short, visible crops are preferable to tall or uncertain surfaces.

why: Radio operation, squawk and SAR phone details are not the urgent occupant safety instructions needed before landing.
Blood types and first-aid location do not replace brace, exit and evacuation directions.
Brief the emergency, pilot’s intentions, safety position, exits/evacuation and post-landing actions.
Teaching checklist use and giving phone numbers is not a concise emergency passenger briefing.
60-053.note: Brief what is happening, brace, exit, and what to do next.

why: Approaching from either side places the person in the tyre’s axial burst path.
A 45-degree angle still approaches from the side-on danger zone.
Approach from the front or rear, avoiding the side-on line where a hot tyre may burst.
The front is safe, but approaching from the right or left enters the tyre’s axial line of fire.
60-054.note: Hot wheels: approach from front or rear, never side-on.

why: Cooling a hot brake with halon is not the relevant precaution and may be unsafe or damaging.
An overheated tyre may burst axially, so keep clear of the wheel’s side-on line of fire.
The keyed hazard is axial bursting, not radial or rotational bursting.
Removing a fairing does not address the tyre-burst hazard and can expose the person to danger.
60-055.note: Keep out of the side-on, axial tyre-burst path.

why: The bank’s defined coverage threshold is 25%, not 50%.
The exam shorthand threshold is 25% coverage; the full definition also specifies contaminant type and depth.
A 10% threshold is below the bank’s stated contaminated-runway coverage threshold.
A 75% threshold is far above the bank’s 25% threshold.
60-056.note: Remember 25% coverage; the full definition also requires >3 mm depth.

why: Standing water increases, rather than decreases, rolling resistance during take-off.
Standing water does not increase lift; it adds drag and can cause aquaplaning.
Water on the runway increases rolling resistance and can compromise acceleration and directional control.
A decrease in lift is not the specific effect asked; standing water increases rolling resistance.
60-057.note: Standing water adds drag and may cause aquaplaning.

why: Adding power and using flaps/spoilers is not the keyed landing-roll response and may compromise control.
Maximum braking can worsen control while hydroplaning; use moderate braking as appropriate.
Crossing rudder and aileron is not a proper braking method and risks loss of directional control.
If wheels are rolling, brake moderately and use aerodynamic means to maintain directional control.
60-058.note: Suspected hydroplaning: moderate braking, maintain directional control.

why: Minimum flaps and no braking do not match the keyed technique; touchdown should be firm.
The keyed touchdown is firm with positive pitch, not negative pitch; brake carefully.
Use minimum crosswind, maximum flap, firm touchdown at minimum safe speed, and careful braking.
This incorrectly uses minimum flaps, soft touchdown and no braking instead of firm touchdown and careful braking.
60-059.note: Use approved data; if unavoidable, minimise crosswind and avoid floating.

why: A glider has no power lever to compensate for bumps; minimise speed and protect the nose with elevator.
Adding approach speed increases impact energy, and pushing the elevator forward at contact is contrary to the keyed technique.
Touch down at minimum speed and hold the elevator back until stopped to protect the glider on the bumpy surface.
Extra approach speed is not needed, and avoiding brakes is not the keyed way to manage the rough landing.
60-060.note: Keyed glider technique: minimum speed, elevator held back through the roll.
